newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso faces key vote on re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso faces key vote on re-election.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, seeking to become Brazil's first re-elected leader, faced the biggest gamble of his political life on Tuesday as a bill allowing him to run again was put to Congress.

The Chamber of Deputies began a session to vote on a constitutional amendment that would give sitting presidents, governors and mayors the right to two consecutive terms and a vote was expected in the early evening, officials said.

"Let's raise a toast to bring us luck," Cardoso said during a lunch with businessmen in the Brazilian capital, shortly before deputies trickled into Congress to begin voting on the controversial bill.

Brazil has banned re-election since the founding of the republic in 1889, mainly to prevent leaders from holding on to power as the country's Portuguese rulers did for centuries. But Cardoso argues the economic reforms he launched as finance minister in 1994 need political continuity to prosper.

If successful, he would join presidents Carlos Menem of Argentina and Alberto Fujimori of Peru as Latin American leaders who have rewritten their countries constitutions to allow their own re-elections.

Government whips said they had overcome resistance to voting on the re-election bill within Cardoso's volatile multi-party alliance in Congress. But they still flew in sick deputies to make sure of the three-fifths majority the bill needs.
"We're gathering more and more votes as time goes by ...We're certain of victory," said Benito Gama, the government's chief whip in the Chamber of Deputies.
The legislation needs to be approved twice in the two houses of Congress, each time by a 60 percent majority.

Opponents from left and right-wing parties, who accuse Cardoso of seeking to further his own political power, buried ideological differences to find ways of obstructing the bill and dismissed the government's upbeat predictions of support.
"What is clear is that we have more-than-enough support to block and stop the voting," Jose Machado, lower house leader of the socialist Workers Party, told national Globo television.

Analysts say the prospect of four more years on top of the two left in his current term would bolster Cardoso's support in Brazil's notoriously fickle Congress. He would then find it easier to push through reforms to streamline the state which have been paralysed for months amid re-election fever.
But if he loses, Cardoso may be unable to maintain control over his unruly allies in the run-up to the 1998 elections, the analysts say.
